title: Orangeville police settle lawsuit surrounding Adam Sprague's jail cell death
article: The family of a man who died in a jail cell at the police station on C Line settled its lawsuit against Orangeville police about five years following his death.

The Banner has confirmed a lawsuit launched by the family of Adam Sprague against the Orangeville Police Service (OPS) was settled outside of court. Further details about the terms of that settlement are not known.

"We can confirm a settlement was reached," Ken Krakar, chair of the Orangeville Police Services Board, advised the Banner in an email. "Any and all terms of the settlement are confidential pursuant to a nondisclosure provision. A press release was not issued in accordance with this nondisclosure provision."
Sprague, who was wrongfully arrested for public intoxication, died of an oxycodone overdose while in a holding cell at the C Line police station early in the morning of Nov. 11, 2010.
Sprague's mother, Margaret, and her other son, Alexander, filed a $1.5 million lawsuit against OPS a little more than a year following his death.

The statement of claim noted Adam's rights were violated when he was arrested for public intoxication on private property on Nov. 10, 2010. The lawsuit also reported OPS staff failed to properly monitor his condition while he was detained in a jail cell overnight.

Following a coroner's inquest, a five-person jury would rule Sprague death was accidental in May of 2014. Along with that verdict, the jury made 33 recommendations for OPS, the local police board and several provincial agencies.
Among them were that OPS physically check on prisoners every 15 minutes. If a prisoner is sleeping, the jury recommended police rouse the person at least every 30 minutes.
Following a probe into Adam's death, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU) announced no criminal charges would be laid against the subject officer investigated.

Const. Jon Kennedy - not the subject officer of that SIU probe - subsequently pleaded guilty to discreditable conduct during a Police Service Act (PSA) hearing, after admitting he made an unlawful arrest. He was ordered to work 24 hours of unpaid duty.

Sgt. Chris Dryden, which the SIU criticized but did not charge criminally for failing to physically check on Sprague in the jail cell overnight, pleaded guilty to two counts of discreditable conduct during a separate PSA hearing in June of 2012.
He was served with a four-month demotion to first-class constable from sergeant for his role in Sprague's death.
The allegations in the Sprague lawsuit have not been proven in court. Krakar has confirmed the matter was settled outside of court on Nov. 14 of 2015.

The Sprague case was settled within one year and a day of a separate lawsuit launched by the family of Heidi Lee Ferguson following her death in September of 2009. The Ferguson lawsuit was settled outside of court on Nov. 15 of last year.
